--- title: "Project 3: Two-Pot Withdrawals" subtitle: "A negative-binomial GLM for behavioural response to a new retirement rule" toc: false number-sections: false execute: echo: false warning: false message: false --- ::: {.pf-meta} | | | |:----|:--------------------------------------------| | Section and topic | Part 2: Time series regression models (non-normal response and indicator variables) | | Type of project | Simulation study with an implementation from first principles, plus a real-data check | | Data used | **Simulated** weekly withdrawal claims calibrated to published SARS figures (no official weekly series is public), and **real** Google Trends interest in "two pot" in South Africa. Period: Sept 2024 to Oct 2026 (112 weeks). All inputs are aggregate and public, so no personal data and no POPIA consent issue. | | Methods used | Negative-binomial regression with an exposure offset, coded as iteratively reweighted least squares with maximum-likelihood dispersion and profiled decay rates, validated against `MASS::glm.nb`; Poisson versus negative-binomial comparison by AIC and dispersion; parameter-recovery and coverage study over 100 simulated series; quasi-Poisson fit to Google Trends. | ::: ## Question Does the Two-Pot rule (one withdrawal per tax year, resetting on 1 March) leave a measurable signature in weekly claims, and what does a Poisson model get wrong about it? ## Key findings
63% vs 70%
reset surge: estimated vs true
342 vs 300
dispersion: estimated vs true
0.84 vs 0.07
interval coverage: negative binomial vs Poisson
353%
reset effect in Google Trends interest
- **Method recovers the truth.** On simulated claims, the estimated reset surge is 63% against a true 70%, and the launch surge is 26% against a true 29%. - **Poisson fails.** Its Pearson dispersion is 341 rather than 1, its AIC is 35,673 higher, and its 95% intervals cover the reset effect 0 of the time in my study against 0.84 for the negative binomial (proportions). - **Estimator validated.** Coefficients match `MASS::glm.nb` to within 1.3e-09. - **Real data.** Google Trends interest shows a reset effect of 353% (95% interval 266% to 462%), with dispersion 0.8. The interval excludes zero, so attention rises at the reset. **What this does and does not show.** The simulation validates the method, not the behavioural story, because the fitted model is the true model. Google Trends measures attention, not claims, so the real-data check is a weak proxy. ![Left: simulated weekly claims with true expected claims and fitted values; dotted lines mark the 1 March resets. Right: profile likelihood for the reset decay rate, with the 95% cut-off and the true value.](figures/p3_headline.png){fig-alt="Two panels: simulated weekly claims with fitted and true curves, and the profile likelihood for the reset decay rate."} ## What I would do differently I would replace the simulation with administrator or FSCA claim data as soon as it exists, since only real counts can test the exhaustion mechanism. I would estimate the decay rates jointly with the other parameters so the standard errors reflect that uncertainty, and add serial correlation through a state-space model, which Project 4 builds. ## Detailed analysis [Read the detailed analysis →](analysis.html){.pf-button} Code and data: [Code & Data appendix](../../appendix/code-and-data.qmd).
